issues.summary: Generic helper function names that don't communicate intent

cloneJSONB, stringifyInstanceID - utility functions without clear domain purpose
messageMetadataBool, isPlaceholderMessageBody - names are descriptive but inconsistent with other helpers
issues.suggestion: Rename helpers to indicate their domain context (e.g., parseUUIDFromPath, parsePaginationParams, parseDateQueryParam). Group related helpers by domain (contact helpers, message helpers, etc.)

issues.summary: Inconsistent naming between resolve/load/get prefixes
evidence: getChatbotSettingsCached vs resolveTemplateAgentName vs loadChatCloseRatingSettings
Mixed use of get, load, resolve, find prefixes without clear distinction
getChatbotFlowsCached, getChatbotFlowByIDCached - 'Cached' suffix only on some functions
issues.suggestion: Establish naming convention: 'get' for simple retrieval, 'load' for database queries, 'resolve' for computed/derived values, 'find' for searches. Add 'Cached' suffix consistently to all cached accessors

issues.summary: Inconsistent abbreviations (org, ctx, req, resp)
evidence: orgID, userID, ctx, req, resp used inconsistently
Some functions use full 'organization', others use 'org'
msg vs message inconsistency (SendOutgoingMessage vs msgReq)
issues.suggestion: Establish standard abbreviations: org (organization), ctx (context), req (request), resp (response). Use consistently or document exceptions. Prefer full names in public APIs

issues.summary: Dead code paths after unconditional returns

Lines 269-274: Duplicate fallback logic in GetAgentComparison - same pattern as GetAgentDetails
Error result from parseDateRange stored but never used before falling back to default
issues.suggestion: Either return the error to the caller or remove the error path entirely. If fallback is intentional, add explanatory comment. Consider extracting date parsing logic to avoid duplication

issues.summary: Redundant nil checks on values that cannot be nil

Line 145: resolveTemplateOrganizationName has similar redundant 'a == nil' checks
Line 228: scheduleContactAvatarRefresh checks 'a == nil' unnecessarily
issues.suggestion: Remove nil checks on method receivers. If defensive programming is needed, use assertions or document preconditions. Consider making these free functions if nil checks are truly needed

issues.summary: Deeply nested conditional logic that's hard to follow

Lines 650-685: parseInboundRatingValue has complex rune-by-rune parsing with nested loops and conditionals
Lines 901-936: extractFollowupCommentsForRatingMessage deeply nested type assertions
issues.suggestion: Extract nested logic into separate functions with clear names. Use early returns to reduce nesting. Consider strategy pattern for type handling

issues.summary: Identical or very similar code in multiple branches
evidence: Lines 546-550: IsSelf check logic duplicated with slight variations
Lines 518-538: parseStatusFont has duplicate error handling patterns
Multiple places have identical error logging patterns
issues.suggestion: Extract common logic to helper functions. Create shared error handling helpers. Use table-driven approaches for repetitive validation

issues.summary: Type assertions on JSONB values without checking ok return
evidence: Line 281: status.Metadata["from_me"].(bool) - only checks ok, ignores false case
Lines 423-437: Multiple type assertions on JSONB with inconsistent ok checking
Line 132: messageMetadataBool does check ok but many other places don't follow this pattern
issues.suggestion: Always check both return values from type assertions. Create helper functions for common JSONB access patterns. Consider using a typesafe wrapper for JSONB

issues.summary: Excessive use of 'any' type loses type safety
evidence: Line 31: Metadata any in ContactResponse - could be structured type
Line 59: Content any in MessageResponse - loses content type information
chat_close_ratings.go: Entries []any in chatCloseRatingFollowupState
issues.suggestion: Define specific types for metadata (e.g., type-safe structs with JSON tags). Use union types or interfaces for Content instead of any. Document the expected structure when any is necessary

issues.summary: Inconsistent UUID handling between string and uuid.UUID types
evidence: stringifyInstanceID converts uuid.UUID to *string but many places need manual string() conversion
InstanceID *string in ContactResponse but should be *uuid.UUID or consistently string
parsePathUUID returns uuid.UUID but many callers immediately call .String()
issues.suggestion: Standardize on uuid.UUID in internal code, convert to string only at API boundaries. Use consistent pointer vs value semantics (prefer value for UUID)

issues.summary: Functions return error without specifying expected error types
evidence: DownloadAndSaveMedia returns error but doesn't document what errors it can return
getChatbotSettingsCached returns error but callers don't distinguish between cache miss, db error, or decrypt error
No custom error types for common failure modes
issues.suggestion: Define custom error types for expected failure modes. Use error wrapping with fmt.Errorf. Document in comments what errors can be returned

issues.summary: Functions perform side effects not indicated by name
evidence: getChatbotSettingsCached: 'get' suggests pure read but it decrypts keys and mutates the settings object
resolveTemplateAgentName: 'resolve' suggests pure function but may update cache
handleManualChatCloseRatingPrompt: sends messages, creates DB records - too much for 'handle'
issues.suggestion: Rename functions to reflect all side effects (e.g., getAndDecryptChatbotSettings, sendAndStoreCloseRatingPrompt). Split functions if they do multiple unrelated things

issues.summary: Functions don't clearly document what they return on error
evidence: findByIDAndOrg: returns error but also sends HTTP response - unclear contract
parsePathUUID: sends error envelope before returning - caller must return nil but this isn't documented
parsePagination: no error case but silently clamps values - unclear if this is intentional
issues.suggestion: Separate validation from response sending. Use sentinel error pattern consistently. Document behavior when input is invalid (clamp vs error vs default)

issues.summary: Functions in same module have different error handling contracts
evidence: Some functions return error and send response (Login), others only send response (CreateAccount)
Inconsistent use of errEnvelopeSent pattern - some check for it, others don't
Mixed use of returning nil vs returning error after sending response
issues.suggestion: Establish standard error handling contract: either always return error OR always send response and return nil. Don't mix patterns in same module

issues.summary: Functions handle nil pointer parameters inconsistently
evidence: Some functions treat nil instanceID as 'filter all', others as error
resolveTemplateAgentName checks for nil contact but other template functions don't
Inconsistent nil handling for *uuid.UUID parameters across codebase
issues.suggestion: Document nil parameter handling in function comments. Use consistent pattern (nil = unfiltered, nil = error, or nil = use default). Consider using functional options pattern for multiple optional params

issues.summary: Inconsistent error handling across modules
evidence: Some functions return errors (cache.go), others send HTTP responses (helpers.go), some log and continue
errEnvelopeSent pattern used in some places but not others
Media functions wrap errors with fmt.Errorf but cache functions return raw errors
issues.suggestion: Choose one error strategy per layer (handlers send responses, services return errors). Use consistent error wrapping. Document error handling strategy for each layer

issues.summary: Errors caught and re-thrown without wrapping original context
evidence: Line 104: decryptChatbotAIKey wraps error but original crypto error context is in message
Line 579: resolveClosePromptAccount returns generic error when multiple things can fail
Many places: errors from DB queries returned directly without adding context about what was being queried
issues.suggestion: Always wrap errors with context using fmt.Errorf or errors.Wrap. Include what operation failed, not just that it failed. Use structured logging with original error

issues.summary: Errors logged but not propagated or recovered from
evidence: Line 301: Failed to update status seen timestamp - logged but operation continues
Line 276: Failed to persist resolved channel name - logged but function continues
Line 447: cache unmarshal errors ignored and treated as cache miss
issues.suggestion: Either propagate the error or explicitly document why it's safe to ignore. For cache, consider corrupted data eviction. For DB updates, consider retry or user notification

issues.summary: Mix of string errors, sentinel errors, and custom error types
evidence: errEnvelopeSent is sentinel error but only used in helpers
String literals used for errors throughout ("Invalid credentials", "Failed to...")
crypto.ErrMissingEncryptionKey is custom error type but other crypto errors are strings
No custom error types for domain-specific failures (auth, validation, etc.)
issues.suggestion: Define custom error types for domain errors. Use sentinel errors for control flow (validation failures). Use string errors only for user-facing messages. Document error type hierarchy

issues.summary: I/O operations without proper error handling
evidence: Line 193: os.WriteFile error wrapped but doesn't handle disk full or permission errors
Line 29: os.MkdirAll error returned but caller doesn't check for specific failures
Line 480: io.ReadAll error handling doesn't distinguish between timeout vs EOF
issues.suggestion: Check for specific I/O error types (os.ErrPermission, os.ErrExist). Handle disk space errors explicitly. Add context about what file/path was being accessed

issues.summary: handlers package contains 147 files with unclear domain boundaries
evidence: The handlers directory contains 147 files including massive files like widgets.go (1403 LOC), contacts.go (1278 LOC), chat_close_ratings.go (1249 LOC), chatbot.go (1360 LOC), and messages.go (1051 LOC)

issues.suggestion: Split handlers into domain subpackages: handlers/contacts, handlers/campaigns, handlers/chatbot, handlers/analytics, handlers/instances, handlers/organizations. Each subpackage should have clear ownership boundaries.

issues.summary: Multiple handler files exceed 1000 LOC indicating poor decomposition
evidence: widgets.go: 1403 LOC, complexity score 158
contacts.go: 1278 LOC, complexity score 177
chat_close_ratings.go: 1249 LOC, complexity score 170
chatbot.go: 1360 LOC, complexity score 141
messages.go: 1051 LOC, complexity score 145
flows.go: 1083 LOC, complexity score 142
issues.suggestion: Break down monolithic files into focused single-responsibility modules. Extract validation, persistence, and business logic into separate packages. Apply Command/Query pattern to reduce handler complexity.

issues.summary: MessageProvider interface creates unnecessary translation layers
evidence: MessageProvider interface defines 10+ methods (SendText, SendImage, SendDocument, SendVideo, SendAudio, MarkRead, SendReaction, RevokeMessage, GetMediaURL, DownloadMedia, UploadMedia)
Both MetaAdapter and WhatsmeowAdapter implement identical interface with only 2 implementations - interface doesn't pay for itself

Direct provider bypassing exists - handlers access WhatsApp client directly instead of using abstraction
issues.suggestion: Consider removing MessageProvider abstraction or merge implementations into a single unified client. The two-provider pattern (Meta vs Whatsmeow) creates more complexity than it solves.

issues.summary: App struct accumulates too many responsibilities and dependencies
evidence: App struct holds 13+ dependencies: Config, DB, Redis, Log, WhatsApp, WhatsmeowStore, WhatsmeowManager, WSHub, Queue, CampaignSubCancel, HTTPClient, MessageProvider, WhatsmeowQueue

getOrgID method contains complex business logic (super-admin override, membership checking) that should be in a domain service
App methods mix concerns: authorization, persistence, WebSocket broadcasting, webhook dispatch, SLA tracking
issues.suggestion: Extract domain services from App into separate packages (orgservice, authservice, contactservice). Handlers should be thin wrappers that delegate to services. App should only hold infrastructure dependencies.

issues.summary: Permission checking scattered and inconsistent across handlers
evidence: Some handlers use: 'if !a.HasPermission(userID, models.ResourceContacts, models.ActionWrite, orgID)'
Others use: 'if err := a.requirePermission(r, userID, models.ResourceAccounts, models.ActionRead); err != nil'
authorizeChatbotRequest returns (uuid.UUID, bool) pattern different from other authorization
No centralized authorization middleware - each handler implements checks independently
issues.suggestion: Implement consistent authorization middleware or helper. Choose one pattern (error return vs bool) and apply uniformly. Consider RBAC middleware that sets context before handlers.

issues.summary: Comments that merely restate the code without adding insight
evidence: // SendText sends a text message - from adapter_send.go line 15
// SendImage sends an image message - from adapter_send.go line 70
// SendDocument sends a document message - from interface.go line 14
// parsePathUUID extracts a UUID from a path parameter - from helpers.go line 18
// endOfDay returns the last nanosecond of the given day - from helpers.go line 81
These comments add no information beyond what the function name already states
issues.suggestion: Remove restating comments. Keep comments that explain WHY not WHAT. For public APIs, document edge cases, preconditions, and invariants instead of repeating names.

issues.summary: Well-designed options pattern for message sending configuration
evidence: MessageSendOptions struct cleanly configures message behavior (BroadcastWebSocket, DispatchWebhook, TrackSLA, ActorType, Async)
DefaultSendOptions(), ChatbotSendOptions(), APISendOptions(), SLASendOptions() provide clear named configurations
resolvedActorType() method encapsulates actor type determination logic
Options pattern avoids function parameter explosion while remaining type-safe
issues.suggestion: Consider applying this options pattern to other complex operations (contact queries, campaign operations). The current design is solid.

issues.summary: MessageProvider adapters are thin wrappers with minimal value-add
evidence: MetaAdapter.SendText: resolve account, then client.SendTextMessage - pure delegation
WhatsmeowAdapter.SendText: getClient, parseJID, simulateTypingIndicator, client.SendMessage - minimal logic

Handlers check provider type explicitly: 'if !a.isWhatsmeowProvider()' pattern throughout codebase

issues.summary: Chat close rating settings parsing duplicated across organization and instance

20+ lines of duplicated type assertion and parsing logic
No extraction of common settings merge logic

issues.summary: JSONB type used throughout without type safety or validation
evidence: models.JSONB used for settings, metadata, context_messages throughout

No compile-time guarantees of setting structure

parseChatCloseRatingWindowDays, parseChatCloseRatingTemplates functions indicate runtime parsing issues

issues.summary: ConnectionManager accumulates responsibilities without clear boundaries

Mixes concerns: client lifecycle, metrics collection, avatar synchronization, call tracking, QR code caching, typing indicators, media queue

SetInboundMediaQueue method suggests dependency injection after construction
issues.suggestion: Split into focused components: ClientPool (connection management), MetricsCollector (metrics), AvatarSyncer (avatars), CallManager (calls), QRCodeCache (caching). Use composition to assemble features.

issues.summary: Identical error handling patterns copied across handlers
evidence: Pattern repeated 20+ times: 'orgID, userID, err := a.getOrgAndUserID(r); if err != nil { return r.SendErrorEnvelope(fasthttp.StatusUnauthorized, "Unauthorized", nil, "") }'
Pattern repeated 15+ times: 'if err := a.requirePermission(r, userID, models.Resource*, models.Action*); err != nil { return nil }'

issues.summary: Request/Response struct pairs duplicated with minor variations

CannedResponseRequest (7 fields) and CannedResponseResponse (10 fields)

ChatbotSettingsResponse with 25+ fields mapping directly to database model

issues.summary: Defensive nil checks on non-nil values throughout codebase

Go doesn't have nil receivers unless called incorrectly - these checks hide bugs
issues.suggestion: Remove nil receiver checks. If called with nil, let it panic - that's a bug to fix. Add nil checks only for interface/pointer parameters that can legitimately be nil.

issues.summary: Helper functions use generic names instead of domain terminology

issues.summary: Struct definitions with extensive field comments but no behavioral documentation

issues.summary: handlers package contains 145 files (50% of entire codebase), creating a hub module with excessive blast radius
